For any support $g$, its contact vector $gu+g'u'$ has scalar components $g$ and $g'$ in the orthonormal frame $(u,u')$. This is why the same vector-distance estimate bounds both errors. Strict finite-stage inequalities can tend to equality: the positive deficits need not have a uniform positive lower bound. solutions.body_md:
On the line $x=h_jn_j+tJn_j$, its intersections with the next and previous support lines have tangent coordinates $(h_{j+1}-h_j\cos\Delta)/\sin\Delta$ and $(h_j\cos\Delta-h_{j-1})/\sin\Delta$. Their difference is $\ell_j$. It is nonnegative: a contact point with $K$ lies between those intersections, and convexly ordered tangent lines bound the circumscribed polygon (zero sides are permitted).

Summation gives $P(P_N)=2\tan(\Delta/2)\sum_jh_j$. Since $h_{j+N/2}+h_j=w$, the sum is $Nw/2$, proving the formula. As the maximum normal gap tends to zero, the circumscribed polygons converge to $K$ (see the mesh-error exercise), and their perimeters tend to $P(K)$. Since $N\tan(\pi/N)\to\pi$, $P(K)=\pi w$.

A sampled normal can lie in a corner's normal cone. Several consecutive supporting lines then meet at that corner, giving indexed side lengths zero; they contribute neither length nor area. Perimeter continuity is used here as an independent fact about planar convex bodies. With that permitted input, the polygon calculation proves Barbier's formula without using it to evaluate the approximating perimeters.

solutions.body_md:
The signed-triangle area identity $A=\frac12\sum h_j\ell_j$ is valid with any origin, by the divergence theorem; substitution yields the quadratic form. The constant part contributes $Nw^2\tan(\pi/N)/4$, and the cross term vanishes since $\sum g_j=0$. For the cyclic quadratic form on $g$, a Fourier mode $e^{imj\Delta}$ has multiplier
$$\frac{\cos(m\Delta)-\cos\Delta}{\sin\Delta}.$$
Antipodal oddness retains only odd $m$. All multipliers are nonpositive, with zero only at $m=1,N-1$. Hence equality means $g_j=a\cos(j\Delta)+b\sin(j\Delta)$, precisely a translation of constant sampled support. The polygon is then regular. The enclosed body need not be a disk: at $N=6$, Pál's theorem supplies a regular supporting hexagon even for a Reuleaux triangle. Letting $N\to\infty$ and using area continuity recovers the disk's maximal-area bound, but this discrete upper bound is not the lower bound of Blaschke–Lebesgue.

The cyclic frequencies are $m=0,\ldots,N-1$. The shift by $N/2$ acts on mode $m$ by $(-1)^m$, explaining exactly why only odd modes occur. Among those frequencies, the largest cosine is $\cos(2\pi/N)$, attained precisely at $m=1,N-1$; thus no other equality modes are hidden. When $N=4$, these are all the allowed modes: every circumscribed four-sided equiangular polygon is a square of side $w$.

solutions.body_md:
Write $h_j=w/2+g_j$. The condition $g_{j+3}=-g_j$ leaves three degrees of freedom. The independent vectors $\cos(j\pi/3)$, $\sin(j\pi/3)$ and $(-1)^j$ form a basis. A translation removes the first two terms. Substitute the remaining $g_j=(-1)^jt$ into the side-length formula with $\cos\Delta=1/2$, $\sin\Delta=\sqrt3/2$ to obtain $\ell_j$. Nonnegative lengths are equivalent to $|t|\leq w/6$.

Summing $\frac12\sum h_j\ell_j$ gives the area formula. The maximum $\sqrt3w^2/2$ occurs at $t=0$, the regular hexagon in Pál's theorem. At $t=\pm w/6$ three alternating sides vanish and the polygon becomes an equilateral triangle of altitude $w$, area $w^2/\sqrt3$. These strip constraints prescribe widths only in three directions; they allow shapes of larger diameter and varying width. Their minimum is therefore below the constant-width minimum and cannot be substituted for it. This illustrates the area-concavity mechanism of the strip-sliding argument in Yaglom–Boltyanskii.

Here an active constraint means its supporting line meets the polygon, even if only at a vertex; this permits the endpoint degeneracies. At $t=\pm w/6$ the equilateral triangle has side length $2w/\sqrt3$ and diameter greater than $w$. It cannot contain a width-$w$ body while all six prescribed support values remain those of that body: prescribing strip separations alone has discarded the full directional-width constraint. Indeed, three of the prescribed supporting lines touch that triangle only at its three vertices. If these were also supports of an enclosed body, that body would have to contain all three vertices, contradicting diameter $w$.

For $x\in P_N$, choose $n_j$ within angle $\Delta/2$ of $x/|x|$. Then $|x|\cos(\Delta/2)\leq x\cdot n_j\leq h_K(n_j)\leq w$, proving confinement. For any unit $u$, choose $n_j$ with $|u-n_j|\leq2\sin(\Delta/4)$. Since $K\subset wB$, its support is $w$-Lipschitz as a function of the unit vector. Consequently
$$x\cdot u-h_K(u)\leq |x|\,|u-n_j|+|h_K(n_j)-h_K(u)|\leq2w(1+\sec(\Delta/2))\sin(\Delta/4).$$
Maximize over $x,u$ and use the support/Hausdorff identity. The bound tends to zero, so convex area continuity proves $A(P_N)\to A(K)$. In particular it applies to $3\cdot2^m$ as $m\to\infty$. Convergence alone gives no lower area bound: one must additionally compare these supporting polygons to the corresponding ones for the Reuleaux triangle, or use the separate polygon-descent proof. The discrete maximum-area calculation and three-strip calculation do not by themselves establish that lower comparison.

The radial estimate is trivial at $x=0$; choose a radial direction only for $x\ne0$. Because $K\subset P_N$, the reverse directed Hausdorff distance is already zero. The uniform support excess bounds precisely the remaining direction, from $P_N$ to $K$. A rate tending to zero is sufficient here; no optimal rate is asserted.
